quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: In natural speech one of these is nearly swallowed. Listen for a short, weak word or for a full, long vowel with a final stop.
quests.explanation: It was "can": a short, weak /kən/ that hides between the other words. "Can't" would open the jaw for a long /ɑː/ and stop on a /t/.
quests.vowelTensionRule: In natural connected speech, unstressed function words like 'can' reduce to /kən/ while negative forms keep a full vowel and final /t/: /kɑːnt/. The reduced form is much shorter and weaker.
quests.mouthPosition: For the weak form keep the mouth relaxed and the vowel a quick schwa. For the strong form open the jaw for /ɑː/ and finish with a firm /t/ or a glottal stop.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: Both fit a page or house number. Where does the beat fall?
quests.explanation: In the sentence, "thirteen" had a strong last syllable with a long /iː/. "Thirty" puts the beat on the first syllable and ends weakly.
quests.vowelTensionRule: -teen sounds like two beats with a strong finish; -ty sounds like one strong beat and a weak tail.
quests.mouthPosition: Tap the beat on the last syllable for -teen, the first for -ty.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: The next word begins with a vowel, so any extra sound at the end will link to it. Listen for a /d/.
quests.explanation: You heard "called": a quick /d/ tucked between the /l/ and the next word. "Call" would run directly from /l/ into the next vowel.
quests.vowelTensionRule: The past-tense -ed ending is pronounced as /t/ after voiceless sounds, /d/ after voiced sounds, and /ɪd/ after /t/ or /d/. Listen for the extra stop at the end.
quests.mouthPosition: Finish the base word, then touch the tongue tip to the ridge for a quick /t/ or /d/. Whisper it after voiceless sounds and voice it after voiced ones.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: Short contracted words are easy to lose in a phrase. Listen for a hush or a breath at the start.
quests.explanation: This time, "she's" began with a hush and rounded lips. "He's" begins with a soft breath.
quests.vowelTensionRule: /ʃ/ is a broad hush made with the tongue raised and the lips rounded; /h/ is only a soft breath from the throat with nothing in the mouth shaping it.
quests.mouthPosition: For /ʃ/ round the lips a little and let air hush over the tongue. For /h/ leave the mouth open and relaxed and just breathe out into the vowel.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: Both make sense here. Is there a hissing tail after the /t/?
quests.explanation: That was "costs": a quick /s/ after the /t/. "Cost" stops at the /t/.
quests.vowelTensionRule: Ask yourself whether the word ends cleanly or with a hiss.
quests.mouthPosition: Make the ending short but audible.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: Where does the loudest, longest part fall?
quests.explanation: In this phrase "sixty" was stressed at the beginning and finished light. "Sixteen" swells on its last syllable.
quests.vowelTensionRule: The vowel in -teen is long and clear; in -ty it is short and weak.
quests.mouthPosition: Smile slightly on the long /iː/ of -teen.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: One word is very short and weak in connected speech. Which one gets more weight?
quests.explanation: The word was "shouldn't": full vowel weight and a nasal-plus-stop ending. "Should" is a light, weak /ʃəd/.
quests.vowelTensionRule: Listen for a full, long vowel and the final /t/ in the negative form.
quests.mouthPosition: Reduce the weak form to almost nothing between the words.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: Does the word have one syllable or two?
quests.explanation: "Waited" has an extra syllable, /ɪd/, at the end. "Wait" stops at the /t/.
quests.vowelTensionRule: The past form adds a short consonant to the end; the base form finishes with the earlier sound.
quests.mouthPosition: Add the tongue-tip closure at the end, even if you don't release it.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: Where does the last strong beat land?
quests.explanation: Here, "eighty" was stressed at the start and ended weakly. "Eighteen" finishes on a long, strong /iː/.
quests.vowelTensionRule: The -teen numbers carry stress on the last syllable (/tiːn/) with a long vowel; the -ty numbers stress the first syllable and end in a weak /ti/. Listen for where the beat falls.
quests.mouthPosition: Stress the second syllable for -teen and lengthen the vowel. Stress the first syllable for -ty and shorten the second.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: Compare the endings: light and quick, or long and rounded?
quests.explanation: It was "carton": a strong first syllable and a weak, quick ending. "Cartoon" ends with a long, stressed /uːn/.
quests.vowelTensionRule: In an unstressed syllable, full vowels shrink to /ə/ or /ɪ/. So a word that differs in stressed vowel will still be clearly different in the strong syllable.
quests.mouthPosition: Stress the first syllable clearly and reduce the second to a relaxed schwa.

quests.instruction: Listen carefully, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: The weak first syllable is the same. Listen to the strong second syllable.
quests.explanation: What you caught was "polite": an /aɪ/ glide and a crisp /t/. "Police" has a long /iː/ and ends with a hiss.
quests.vowelTensionRule: The stressed syllable carries the contrast, so focus on it rather than on the weak ending.
quests.mouthPosition: Tap on the strong syllable and let the rest fade.

quests.instruction: Listen carefully, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: The first syllable is weak in both. Is there a nasal hum at the start?
quests.explanation: "Event" starts with a short, unstressed /ɪ/ that goes straight to /v/. "Invent" has a small /n/ hum before the /v/.
quests.vowelTensionRule: One word has an extra little sound or syllable in an unstressed spot. That weak piece is short and quiet, but it changes the rhythm of the word, so listen for it before or after the strong beat.
quests.mouthPosition: Keep the stressed syllable strong and clear, then add or leave out the weak piece with a relaxed tongue. Don't let it grow louder than the beat.

quests.instruction: Listen carefully, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: Where does the /s/ belong: with the first word or the second?
quests.explanation: You heard "ice cream": the /s/ closes the first word and the /k/ is breathy. In "I scream" the /s/ joins the next word and the /k/ is soft.
quests.vowelTensionRule: Word boundaries in fast speech are marked by tiny changes in timing and aspiration rather than by pauses. A /s/ that belongs to the next word makes the following stop unaspirated, and an /n/ can slide onto the next vowel.
quests.mouthPosition: Say the phrase as one smooth rhythm, but keep the tongue and lip positions of each word. Notice whether the consonant sits at the end of one word or the start of the next.

quests.instruction: Listen carefully, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: Does a nasal hum sit at the end of the first word or the start of the second?
quests.explanation: "a name" starts the second word with an /n/, tongue tip on the ridge. In "an aim" the /n/ ends the first word and the next word starts with a vowel.
quests.vowelTensionRule: Word boundaries in fast speech are marked by tiny changes in timing and aspiration rather than by pauses. A /s/ that belongs to the next word makes the following stop unaspirated, and an /n/ can slide onto the next vowel.

quests.vowelTensionRule: Word boundaries in fast speech are marked by tiny changes in timing and aspiration rather than by pauses. A /s/ that belongs to the next word makes the following stop unaspirated, and an /n/ can slide onto the next vowel.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: The next word starts with a vowel, so an extra sound will link. Is there a /d/ after the /n/?
quests.explanation: It was "opened", with a quick /d/ after the /n/ joining the next word. "Open" ends on the /n/.
quests.vowelTensionRule: A short /t/ or /d/ closes the past-tense word, and it may be unreleased before a consonant.
quests.mouthPosition: Keep the ending short and soft.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: One word is much lighter. Which has a nasal and a stop at the end?
quests.explanation: This time, "don't" had a gliding vowel plus /nt/. "Do" is a light, quick /də/ or /du/.
quests.vowelTensionRule: A stressed, full vowel usually signals the negative.
quests.mouthPosition: Give the negative form its full vowel and hold it longer.

quests.instruction: Listen carefully, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: Does the word start with a hiss straight into the /p/, or with a weak vowel first?
quests.explanation: What you caught was "support": a weak /sə/ came first and the /p/ was breathy. In "sport" the /s/ and /p/ are joined together.
quests.vowelTensionRule: One word has an extra little sound or syllable in an unstressed spot. That weak piece is short and quiet, but it changes the rhythm of the word, so listen for it before or after the strong beat.

quests.mouthPosition: Tap the beat on the last syllable for -teen, the first for -ty.

quests.instruction: Listen to the phrase, then select the word you hear.

quests.vowelTensionRule: One word has an extra little sound or syllable in an unstressed spot. That weak piece is short and quiet, but it changes the rhythm of the word, so listen for it before or after the strong beat.

quests.vowelTensionRule: The past-tense -ed ending is pronounced as /t/ after voiceless sounds, /d/ after voiced sounds, and /ɪd/ after /t/ or /d/. Listen for the extra stop at the end.

quests.hint: Same sounds, different rhythm. Which syllable gets the beat?
quests.explanation: You heard "insight": the first syllable was strong and the second weak. "Incite" puts the beat on the second syllable.
quests.vowelTensionRule: Stress placement is audible as a change in pitch, length and loudness.
quests.mouthPosition: Relax the mouth on the unstressed syllable so the vowel becomes a quick /ə/.

quests.mouthPosition: Add the tongue-tip closure at the end, even if you don't release it.

quests.instruction: Listen carefully, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: Listen for a buzz at the end.
quests.explanation: It was "goes": a soft /z/ at the end. "Go" ends on the vowel.
quests.vowelTensionRule: The final /s/ or /z/ adds a whole extra sound to the end of the word, creating a consonant cluster. Listen for a hissing or buzzing tail after the word.
quests.mouthPosition: End the base word cleanly, then add a quick /s/ or /z/ with the tongue tip near the ridge. Voice the ending after voiced sounds and whisper it after voiceless ones.

quests.instruction: Listen carefully, then select the word you hear.
quests.hint: Which syllable is strongest?
quests.explanation: "Discuss" has the beat on the second syllable, with a full /ʌ/. "Discus" has the beat on the first syllable and a weak ending.
quests.vowelTensionRule: English stress changes vowel quality and length: the stressed syllable is louder, longer and clearer, while unstressed syllables reduce toward /ə/ or /ɪ/. The words differ in where the strong syllable falls.
quests.mouthPosition: Make the stressed syllable longer, louder and slightly higher in pitch, and let the other syllable shrink.
